donors.name: African Development Bank Group (AfDB)
donors.shortDescription: Africa's regional development bank, financing infrastructure, agriculture, industrialisation and regional integration across the continent.
donors.overview:
The African Development Bank Group finances development in its African member countries through the African Development Bank (lending on market-based terms), the African Development Fund (concessional finance for lower-income countries) and the Nigeria Trust Fund.

Its strategic priorities, known as the 'High 5s', are to light up and power Africa, feed Africa, industrialise Africa, integrate Africa, and improve the quality of life for the people of Africa.

The Bank also manages several thematic trust funds and initiatives on climate, gender and youth entrepreneurship.
donors.howToPartner:
Like other development banks, the AfDB lends mainly to governments and to private sector projects. Civil society and smaller organisations usually engage through Bank-financed projects, procurement, or specific funds and initiatives that issue calls.

Check the Bank's project portal for operations in your country and its procurement notices.
donors.source: Unverified demo draft. Original demo source label: AfDB official website

donors.name: Deutsche Gesellschaft für Internationale Zusammenarbeit (GIZ)
donors.shortDescription: Germany's federally owned enterprise for international cooperation, implementing technical cooperation projects mainly on behalf of the German government.
donors.overview:
GIZ is a federal enterprise that implements international cooperation projects, mainly commissioned by the German Federal Ministry for Economic Cooperation and Development (BMZ). It also works for other German ministries, the European Union and other public and private clients.

GIZ is an implementing agency rather than a classic donor. Its strength is technical cooperation: advisory services, capacity development, and long-term programmes with partner governments in areas such as vocational training, energy, climate, governance and sustainable economic development.

GIZ is present in many countries through country offices, which makes local engagement possible.
donors.howToPartner:
Organisations can work with GIZ as implementing partners, grant recipients (local subsidies or financing agreements under specific projects), or service providers through GIZ tenders.

Private companies can explore the develoPPP programme, which co-finances development partnerships with the private sector. The best entry point is usually the GIZ country office and the projects already running in your sector.

donors.name: European Commission – DG International Partnerships (INTPA)
donors.shortDescription: The European Commission department that designs EU development policy and funds partnerships in Africa, Asia, the Pacific, Latin America and the Caribbean.
donors.overview:
DG INTPA is the European Commission's Directorate-General responsible for international partnerships. It manages a large share of the EU's external funding under the Global Europe instrument (NDICI-Global Europe) for Sub-Saharan Africa, Asia, the Pacific, Latin America and the Caribbean.

The EU's flagship investment strategy, Global Gateway, focuses on digital, climate and energy, transport, health, and education and research. Alongside large investment programmes, DG INTPA funds civil society, human rights, governance and thematic programmes.

The EU works in a 'Team Europe' approach, combining resources from EU institutions, Member States and European development finance institutions. Much of the programming is managed by EU Delegations in partner countries.
donors.howToPartner:
Grants are awarded mainly through calls for proposals published on the EU Funding & Tenders portal. Applicants usually need to register in the EU's system and often apply in consortia with co-applicants. Calls frequently require co-financing from the applicant.

For country-level opportunities, follow the EU Delegation in your country, which publishes local calls for civil society and human rights programmes.
donors.source: Unverified demo draft. Original demo source label: European Commission – International Partnerships website

donors.name: Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office (FCDO)
donors.shortDescription: The UK government department that manages most of the UK's official development assistance alongside its diplomatic work.
donors.overview:
The FCDO was created in 2020 by merging the UK's Foreign and Commonwealth Office with the Department for International Development. It manages most UK official development assistance (ODA), combining development, diplomacy and security objectives.

The UK government has announced a reduction of its aid budget to 0.3% of gross national income by 2027, so programme portfolios are changing. Recent priorities include humanitarian response, global health, climate, girls' education and economic development.

Many FCDO programmes are delivered through large implementing partners and fund managers that run their own grant windows for local organisations.
donors.howToPartner:
FCDO publishes procurement opportunities through UK government contract portals, and many grant funds are run by appointed fund managers. Local organisations usually access FCDO funding as sub-grantees or consortium members.

The UK's Development Tracker website lists active programmes by country, which helps identify implementing partners to approach.
donors.source: Unverified demo draft. Original demo source label: UK Government website

donors.name: Gates Foundation
donors.shortDescription: One of the world's largest private foundations, focused on global health, agricultural development, gender equality and US education.
donors.overview:
The Gates Foundation is a private philanthropic foundation based in Seattle. It funds work on global health (including vaccines, polio eradication, maternal and child health and infectious diseases), agricultural development, gender equality, and education in the United States.

In 2025 the foundation announced that it plans to spend most of its resources over the following two decades and close by 2045, with a strong focus on ending preventable deaths of mothers and babies, eliminating deadly infectious diseases, and lifting people out of poverty.

The foundation works closely with governments, multilateral organisations and global health partnerships, and funds research and innovation.
donors.howToPartner:
Most Gates Foundation grants are made by invitation, after programme staff identify partners that fit a specific strategy. Unsolicited proposals are generally not accepted.

Open opportunities exist through specific requests for proposals and innovation programmes such as Grand Challenges. Read the strategy for your area of work to see whether your project aligns.
donors.source: Unverified demo draft. Original demo source label: Gates Foundation official website

donors.name: Green Climate Fund (GCF)
donors.shortDescription: The world's largest dedicated climate fund, supporting developing countries to reduce emissions and adapt to climate change.
donors.overview:
The Green Climate Fund was set up under the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) and is headquartered in Songdo, Republic of Korea. It aims to invest equally in climate mitigation and adaptation, with a strong share of adaptation funding going to the most vulnerable countries.

GCF provides grants, concessional loans, equity and guarantees. Projects are submitted and implemented by Accredited Entities, which include UN agencies, development banks, national institutions and some NGOs.

Each country has a National Designated Authority (NDA) that acts as the focal point and must give a no-objection letter for projects in that country.
donors.howToPartner:
Organisations work with GCF either by becoming an Accredited Entity (a demanding process), or more often by partnering with an existing Accredited Entity and the country's National Designated Authority.

The GCF Readiness Programme funds capacity building and country programming, and is a good entry point for national institutions.
donors.source: Unverified demo draft. Original demo source label: Green Climate Fund official website

donors.name: International Fund for Agricultural Development (IFAD)
donors.shortDescription: A UN specialised agency and international financial institution investing in rural people, smallholder farmers and food systems.
donors.overview:
IFAD, based in Rome, is both a specialised agency of the United Nations and an international financial institution. It provides loans and grants to governments to finance rural development programmes that raise the incomes and resilience of smallholder farmers and rural communities.

Its work covers agricultural productivity, access to markets and finance, climate adaptation for small-scale agriculture, nutrition, and the inclusion of women, youth and Indigenous Peoples.

IFAD's resources come from member-state replenishments, and it increasingly mobilises co-financing and private-sector investment for rural development.
donors.howToPartner:
IFAD's main partners are governments, which implement IFAD-financed projects. NGOs, farmers' organisations and research institutions take part as service providers or implementing partners within those projects, and IFAD issues some grant calls for regional and global initiatives.

The project list on IFAD's website shows active investments by country.

donors.name: Japan International Cooperation Agency (JICA)
donors.shortDescription: Japan's development agency, combining technical cooperation, concessional loans and grant aid, with a strong presence in Asia and Africa.
donors.overview:
JICA implements most of Japan's official development assistance. It brings together three main tools: technical cooperation (experts, training and capacity development), ODA loans for large investments such as transport and energy infrastructure, and grant aid.

JICA has a long history in Asia and a growing portfolio in Africa, linked to the Tokyo International Conference on African Development (TICAD). Priority areas include infrastructure, health, education, agriculture, disaster risk reduction and peacebuilding.

JICA also runs volunteer programmes and partnerships with Japanese NGOs, local governments, universities and companies.
donors.howToPartner:
JICA mostly works government-to-government, so national ministries are its main partners. NGOs can partner through the JICA Partnership Program, which is designed mainly for Japanese organisations, often working with local partners.

In partner countries, the JICA office is the entry point for understanding which programmes are active.

donors.name: Mastercard Foundation
donors.shortDescription: A private foundation focused on youth employment and education in Africa, and on Indigenous youth in Canada.
donors.overview:
The Mastercard Foundation is an independent foundation based in Toronto. Its main strategy, Young Africa Works, aims to enable millions of young people in Africa, particularly young women, to access dignified and fulfilling work by 2030.

The foundation works through partnerships with governments, education institutions, financial service providers and businesses, often at country level in its priority countries. Its Scholars Program supports talented young people with limited financial means to pursue secondary and higher education.

In Canada, the foundation's EleV program works with Indigenous youth and communities on education and employment.

The foundation generally identifies partners proactively and does not accept unsolicited proposals in most areas. Opportunities appear as targeted calls, challenge funds or partnerships within its country strategies.

Organisations working on youth employment in its priority African countries can follow its country programmes and partner organisations.

donors.name: Swedish International Development Cooperation Agency (Sida)
donors.shortDescription: Sweden's government agency for development cooperation, funding work on democracy, human rights, gender equality and climate.
donors.overview:
Sida is a government agency under the Swedish Ministry for Foreign Affairs. It manages most of Sweden's bilateral development aid and humanitarian assistance, working through country and regional strategies decided by the Swedish government.

Sida rarely implements projects itself. It funds partners such as civil society organisations, UN agencies, multilateral organisations, research institutions and, in some cases, partner governments. Long-term support to strategic partners, including core funding for civil society organisations, has been a distinctive feature of Swedish aid.

Swedish development cooperation has been reformed in recent years, with stronger links to trade, migration and support to Ukraine. Participants should read the current country or thematic strategy before approaching Sida, because funding is tied to these strategies.
donors.howToPartner:
Most Sida funding goes through framework and strategic partner organisations rather than open calls. Smaller organisations usually access Sida funds indirectly, for example through Swedish civil society organisations that hold framework agreements, or through Swedish embassies in partner countries that manage the bilateral strategy.

Check the relevant country strategy, then contact the Swedish embassy's development section or a Swedish framework organisation working in your sector.
donors.source: Unverified demo draft. Original demo source label: Sida official website

donors.name: The Global Fund to Fight AIDS, Tuberculosis and Malaria
donors.shortDescription: A global partnership that raises and invests funds to end AIDS, tuberculosis and malaria and to strengthen health systems.
donors.overview:
The Global Fund is a partnership of governments, civil society, technical agencies, the private sector and people affected by the diseases. Based in Geneva, it raises money in three-year replenishment cycles and allocates it to eligible countries.

Funding is channelled through country-owned processes. In each country, a Country Coordinating Mechanism (CCM), which includes government, civil society, communities and partners, prepares funding requests and oversees grants. Grants are managed by Principal Recipients, which can be government bodies, NGOs or UN agencies.

Beyond the three diseases, the Global Fund invests in resilient health systems, community systems, and pandemic preparedness.
donors.howToPartner:
Organisations cannot apply directly to the Global Fund outside the country process. The main entry points are the Country Coordinating Mechanism in your country and the Principal Recipients, which subcontract Sub-Recipients to implement activities.

Community and civil society organisations are expected to take part in the CCM's country dialogue when funding requests are prepared.

donors.name: United Nations Development Programme (UNDP)
donors.shortDescription: The UN's development agency, present in around 170 countries and territories, working on poverty, governance, climate and crisis recovery.
donors.overview:
UNDP supports countries to eradicate poverty, reduce inequalities and build resilience. Its work covers democratic governance, climate and environment, energy, crisis prevention and recovery, and support to national SDG planning.

UNDP is both a funding channel and an implementer. It manages large programmes funded by governments, the EU, vertical funds such as the Global Environment Facility and the Green Climate Fund, and pooled funds.

It often works as a convener between governments, civil society and the private sector, and it hosts the UN Volunteers programme and the UN Capital Development Fund.
donors.howToPartner:
Civil society organisations can become UNDP responsible parties or grant recipients under specific projects, usually selected through calls published by the country office. UNDP also runs the GEF Small Grants Programme, which funds community-based environmental projects.

Governments and donors engage with UNDP through cost-sharing agreements. Procurement opportunities are published on UN procurement platforms.
donors.source: Unverified demo draft. Original demo source label: UNDP official website

donors.name: World Bank Group
donors.shortDescription: A family of international financial institutions providing loans, grants, guarantees and knowledge to governments and the private sector in developing countries.
donors.overview:
The World Bank Group includes the International Bank for Reconstruction and Development (IBRD), which lends to middle-income countries, and the International Development Association (IDA), which provides grants and highly concessional credits to the poorest countries. The International Finance Corporation (IFC) and MIGA work with the private sector.

The Bank finances large programmes in infrastructure, health, education, social protection, agriculture and climate, and produces widely used research and data.

Its main counterparts are national governments. Civil society organisations engage mainly through consultations, as implementing partners within government projects, or through specific trust funds and grant programmes.
donors.howToPartner:
Most World Bank funding flows through governments, so the most realistic route for NGOs and consultants is to engage with Bank-financed national projects, for example through procurement notices published by implementing ministries.

The World Bank's projects database lets you search active and pipeline operations by country and sector.
